headline: `pki.cmp.verify` reads every option at the call, so a caller that reuses its options object while verification runs cannot change the verdict that call returns.
summary: Verifying a CMP message suspends the call -- PBMAC1 derivation on the MAC path, the signature engine on the other. Five options were read after it resumed, so they answered for whatever the caller last wrote rather than for the call that was made. A caller could pass a transaction identifier the message does not carry, overwrite the buffer while the MAC derived, and be told the message was valid.

Fixed: `pki.cmp.verify` reduces every option to a value the caller no longer reaches, before verification begins. `transactionID` and `expectRecipNonce` are copied, so overwriting the buffer that was passed in changes nothing; `trustAnchors` and `intermediates` have their array copied, so appending an anchor mid-call cannot widen the set the chain is built against; and a `time` that is a real `Date` is re-made at the same instant, so calling `setTime` on it cannot move the point the signer's certificate is validated at. A `time` that is not a `Date` passes through untouched, so the input error it already earns is the one it still gets.

Each option is read from the caller's object exactly once and copied in the same step, before the next option is read. A property can be an accessor: asked twice it may answer differently, so the value that passed the check would not be the value that was used; and an accessor invoked for a later option can reach back and rewrite the buffer an earlier one handed over, so reading the whole bag before copying any of it would copy whatever the last accessor left behind.

A certificate list is copied by the elements it holds rather than by walking its `length`. The two are independent, so a sparse list carrying one certificate at index 100000000 costs nothing to build and would have cost a dense hundred-million-entry copy inside `verify`; it now collapses to the one certificate it carries. No ceiling is imposed on how many anchors a caller may supply.

Two things stay caller-owned by design, and the release is explicit about them. A parsed certificate passed as an anchor or an intermediate is held by reference, because `pki.schema.x509.parse` results carry their provenance against the object's identity and a copy would stop being recognized as parser output; editing one mid-call changes nothing, since path validation re-derives a parsed certificate from the bytes it recorded. And a `revocationChecker` is the caller's own callback, so what it answers is theirs to decide whenever it is called.
